q-122491:
In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

Substituting $n=6$ and $r=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{6}{C}_{3} & =\frac{6!}{(6-3)!\,3!} \\  & =\frac{6!}{3!\,3!} \\  & =\frac{6\cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot \cancel{3!}}{\cancel{3!}3!} \\  & =\frac{6\cdot 5\cdot 4}{6} \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

q-85044:
First, note that $(\frac{20}{16})$ means the same thing as ${}_{20}{C}_{16}.$

 In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

Substituting $n=20$ and $r=16,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{20}{C}_{16} & =\frac{20!}{(20-16)!16!} \\  & =\frac{20!}{4!16!} \\  & =\frac{20\cdot 19\cdot 18\cdot 17\cdot \cancel{16!}}{4!\cancel{16!}} \\  & =\frac{20\cdot 19\cdot 18\cdot 17}{4\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{116\,280}{24} \\  & =4\,845.\end{aligned}
$$

q-122498:
First, note that $(\frac{7}{6})$ means the same thing as ${}_{7}{C}_{6}.$

 In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

Substituting $n=7$ and $r=6,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{7}{C}_{6} & =\frac{7!}{(7-6)!6!} \\  & =\frac{7!}{1!6!} \\  & =\frac{7\cdot \cancel{6!}}{1\cdot \cancel{6!}} \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

q-84956:
The number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

There are $9$ toppings, so $n=9.$ We want to select $3$ of those toppings for each of the pizzas, so we have $r=3.$

Therefore, the number of different pizzas is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{9}{C}_{3} & =\frac{9!}{(9-3)!\,3!} \\  & =\frac{9!}{6!3!} \\  & =\frac{9\cdot 8\cdot 7\cdot \cancel{6!}}{\cancel{6!}3!} \\  & =\frac{9\cdot 8\cdot 7}{3\cdot 2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{504}{6} \\  & =84.\end{aligned}
$$

q-122551:
The number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

There are $7$ days in a week, so $n=7.$ We want to select $5$ of those days for Mike to workout, so we have $r=5.$

Therefore, the number of choices is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{7}{C}_{5} & =\frac{7!}{(7-5)!\,5!} \\  & =\frac{7!}{2!5!} \\  & =\frac{7\cdot 6\cdot \cancel{5!}}{2!\cancel{5!}} \\  & =\frac{7\cdot 6}{2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{42}{2} \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

q-5571:
In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

There are $15$ questions, so $n=15.$ We want to select $10$ of those questions to answer, so we have $r=10.$

Therefore, the number of ways to answer $10$ different questions is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{15}{C}_{10} & =\frac{15!}{(15-10)!\,10!} \\  & =\frac{15!}{5!10!} \\  & =\frac{15\cdot 14\cdot 13\cdot 12\cdot 11\cdot \cancel{10!}}{5!\cancel{10!}} \\  & =\frac{15\cdot 14\cdot 13\cdot 12\cdot 11}{5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{360\,360}{120} \\  & =3\,003.\end{aligned}
$$

q-1781:
In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

There are $80$ people, so $n=80.$ We want to select $4$ of those people for each group, so we have $r=4.$

Therefore, the number of different potential groups of four is

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{80}{C}_{4} & =\frac{80!}{(80-4)!\,4!} \\  & =\frac{80!}{76!4!} \\  & =\frac{80\cdot 79\cdot 78\cdot 77\cdot \cancel{76!}}{\cancel{76!}4!} \\  & =\frac{80\cdot 79\cdot 78\cdot 77}{4\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{37\,957\,920}{24} \\  & =1\,581\,580.\end{aligned}
$$

q-124611:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{5}{9}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{5}{9} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{4}{9} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $x=\frac{2}{3}.$

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ 2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =2-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =2-2{(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4})}^{2} \\  & =2-2(\frac{10}{16}) \\  & =2-\frac{20}{16} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So our final answer is $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{4}.$

$$

$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{5}{9}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{5}{9})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{25}{81}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{56}{81}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{14}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So our final answer is $sin⁡\theta =\frac{2\sqrt{14}}{9}.$

$$

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{3}{9}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{6}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.$

Knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3})}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}}.
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡\theta  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{6} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

q-100449:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base.

To do this, we write $64$ as ${8}^{2},$ and then we rewrite the right-hand side using the power rule of exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{5a-12} & =\frac{1}{{64}^{a+4}} \\ {8}^{5a-12} & =\frac{1}{{({8}^{2})}^{a+4}} \\ {8}^{5a-12} & =\frac{1}{{8}^{2(a+4)}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using a negative exponent: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{5a-12} & ={8}^{-2(a+4)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(8)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5a-12 & =-2(a+4) \\ 5a-12 & =-2a-8 \\ 7a & =4 \\ a & =\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$
